Photograph: Sem van der Wal/EPA Museums Guns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says Europol EU police agency says shift could point to involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific artefacts Sam Jones Mon 24 Aug 2026 10.31 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 12.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way into buildings and display cases, according to a report by Europol. The EU police agency said that while museum thefts were generally seen as a non-violent form of organised property crime, member states had detected a recent shift “towards violent and forceful methods” that could point to the involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific cultural artefacts. The report says: “Unlike typical cultural goods traffickers, who usually avoid violence and specialise in organised property crime or the theft of cultural goods, these individuals often have histories of involvement in other types of crime. “Additionally, some thieves apprehended in recent cases appear to coordinate their efforts on an ad hoc basis, often recruited locally through social media and instant communication channels, without prior connections to each other. This differs from the usual structure of criminal networks involved in cultural goods trafficking, which typically operate in a core group organised around a leader.” View image in fullscreen Police outside the Louvre in Paris, where there was a heist last October. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters The report, published on Monday, found that precious metals and jewellery were the preferred targets because of their increasing value and the ease with which gold and silver could be melted down and jewels removed from their settings. “Similarly, ancient Chinese porcelain artefacts are likely targeted by cultural goods traffickers for financial gain,” it says. “Driven by high demand, they are likely to be easily sold on the art market.” Europol said a number of recent heists showed some thieves had few qualms when it came to using explosives or employing violence. In January 2025, a gang blasted its way into the Drents Museum in the Netherlands and stole several Dacian artefacts , many of which were subsequently recovered. The report adds: “In some cases, offenders use firearms to intimidate security personnel and visitors. Some museum thefts have involved direct physical assaults on staff such as tying them up or using brute force against them. Across reported cases, the use of force is closely linked to targeted operations, suggesting prior identification of specific objects and preplanned execution.” It pointed out that four hooded suspects equipped with baseball bats and axes had stolen seven gold and diamond-adorned objects from the Cognacq-Jay art museum in Paris in 2024, while the heist at the Louvre in October 2025 had involved similar violence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “To access the targeted artefacts, the [Louvre] thieves broke a window and threatened guards and visitors,” the report says. “They smashed the display cases in the Apollo Gallery, and stole jewellery worth an estimated €88m.” Europol said that while more evidence needed to be gathered, it was possible low-level museum thieves were being randomly recruited “on a crime-as-a-service basis”. It added: “Alternatively, some criminal actors and networks, typically active in other criminal markets, [have] realised the low-risk, high-profit potential of museum heists.” Explore more on these topics Museums Europe Police Organised crime European Union news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Mastermind of €88m Louvre heist thought they ‘could have taken more’ Macron appoints new head of crisis-hit Louvre after jewellery heist Louvre president resigns as jewellery heist inquiry reveals ‘systemic failures’ Alleged cat burglar arrested after priceless Egyptian artefacts taken in Queensland museum heist The Louvre is the pride of France – and it’s on the verge of collapse. By Paulin Kola Â and Â Joe Coughlan Published 25 August 2026 US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East. "Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. There is no comment from Iran. Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran. In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf. A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran. However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated. Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied. However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime. Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US. Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue. On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights. The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month. Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products. Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US. Iran, for its part, has indicated that it wants to establish full control of the Strait of Hormuz - a view that is opposed by the US and most other countries which believe that the passage constitutes international waters and transit should remain unimpeded as it was before the war. Until recently - and on the basis of the MoU - Iran had been involved in negotiations with Oman, a US ally, to agree a mechanism for administering the strait. However, those talks have so far not produced an agreement and, last week, Trump even threatened to bomb its ally "if it gets in the way" of his administration's own talks with Iran over the issue. Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the strait after meeting his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran. He said in a statement he also hoped for "practical arrangements" to restore safe navigation, adding: "Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course." Araghchi confirmed the meeting in a statement, saying "regional solutions" were discussed in talks with representatives from Pakistan and Oman. He added that discussions covered the future management of the strait, as well as the framework for a new corridor and a joint mine-clearing operation. Speaking to state television news after the meeting Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabad said the entry route to the Gulf would be "through Iranian waters and the exit route through Omani territorial waters, and ships will pass through Iranian waters on both routes". The minister added that the south corridor of the waterway, which has been recommended to shipping firms by the US and is situated close to the coast of Oman , would be "closed" under the framework, and the meeting "does not mean that the Strait will be opened from tomorrow". He said "no military vessels will be allowed to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, and only commercial vessels will be allowed to pass through it". Gharibabad called the route "temporary", adding Iran and Oman will negotiate a new permanent route within a timeframe of 60 days to replace the previous maritime traffic plan. "If Iran's requests are not granted, the Strait will be closed," he said. Beállítom Gyomorszájon és fejen lőtték szeptember harmadikán csütörtökön reggel Nyikolaj Verpahovicsot, az orosz légierő tábornokát – írja a TASZSZ és orosz katonai blogok alapján a Meduza. Ukrajna őt tartja felelősnek a kijevi Ohmatdyt gyermekklinika elleni 2024-es rakétatámadásért. Nyikolaj Verpahovics az orosz légierő 22. nehézbombázó repülőhadosztályának parancsnoka. Az ukrán biztonsági szolgálat és az ukrán legfőbb ügyészség szerint ő adta ki a parancsot, hogy az orosz hadsereg 2024. július 8-án rakétákkal lője a kijevi Ohmatdyt Gyermekkórházat, amelyben akkor 600 beteg és körülbelül ugyanannyi alkalmazott tartózkodott. Az akkori támadásban két ember meghalt. Szeptember 3-án csütörtök reggel Verpahovics Oroszország Szaratov régiójában, a Szaratov melletti Probuzsgyenije faluban tartózkodott, amikor egy támadó egy motorral mellé hajtott, és kétszer rálőtt. Az egyik lövés a gyomorszáját, a másik a fejét találta el. A támadó ezután elhajtott a helyszínéről. Verpahovics a helyszínen nem vesztette életét, a sofőrje mentőt hívott hozzá, a mentők ellátták és jelenleg előkészítik, hogy egy moszkvai kórházba szállíthassák.
